p:
Thank you for the question, Council Member. Well, my understanding

at the time is the First Deputy Mayor's office actually ended up taking the lead on engaging with the industry on winding down pursuant to the executive order. And I know they engaged in active conversations, particularly with labor partners, but also had staff operating in the field in Central Park to liaise with workers. That's my understanding of the touchpoint of what Mayor's– the Adams administration ended up doing under that executive order.
So that's not the responsibility of DCW to reach out, the carriage workers?

We work closely with them to provide them contact information, data, and then the mayor's office ended up taking the lead on the next steps on that. You know, I think as I mentioned as well earlier in my testimony, workforce development is not necessarily something that DCWP currently administers or engages in. There are other agencies across the city that do that work, and I think are part of the conver— a part of the administration's now response to implementing this bill. Alright, thank you. Question on the— for

DOHMH. Your agency has been responsible for inspecting and licensing carriage horses in the city. The horse rider was cleared as fit to work, yet was found to be nearly 30 years old and suffering from a neurological pathological disease. The horse Lady died in the street. Another horse Deniz died in the park. Question, how many inspections were conducted on each of these horses in the 12 months before their deaths? And what did those inspections actually find? Please answer that.

So, for Deniz, I did want to note that our– the report following Deniz's death, as everyone will probably remember, was that that horse had ingested a toxic plant. And I did want to highlight that our course for drivers includes the Parks Department requirement that horses not disturb the vegetation.
Okay, thank you.
Well, there were— were there any inspections done on these horses–
[interposing] So we can pull up—
before they died?
We can pull up the certifications that the horses' veterinarians would have provided to us in order to be licensed.
Okay, thank you very much. Council Member Ariola?
Thank you, Chair, and thank you for coming to testify. So I have a question. I would want to go back to the vet. Who is the contracted vet for the Department of Health?
We have multiple contracted veterinarians.
Okay. Who would be one that is a large animal veterinarian, an equine veterinarian?
The veteran— the veterinarians— we have other veterinarians. The veterinarians I've been speaking about are equine veterinarians.
Do you know the names of those veterinarians? Or the one that you mo— use most of the time?
There are multiple veterinarians that— equine veterinarians that we work with.
And do you have their names?
I would rather not provide their names here.
Why would that be?
The equine veterinarians work with us at the Health Department under contract, and I would prefer not to provide their names.

Is the reason why you do not want to provide their names is because they have been suspended in the past, or relieved from their position at the ASPCA, or have any type of history of using steroids in horses, or submitting certificates that— of examination for horses to the department without doing those exams? Would that be why you wouldn't want to mention their names?
I'm not aware of those– the implications that you're making. I don't— I'm trying to protect their privacy.

This is an issue that is very important because part and parcel of why this legislation is so important is because we're just as concerned about the health of the horses, the

health and well-being of the horses, and if we have compromised veterinarians that are checking the health of the horses before they're going out onto the street, then that is a problem. That is why it's important that this committee— and perhaps you'd like to share those names with the Chair privately so that it's not made public.

I understand. I appreciate that. I do want to say that the veterinarians– the veterinarians that certify the horses as fit to work are are not Health Department veterinarians. Those are the veterinarians that the owners engage to be the veterinarians for their own horses. And I don't have— I don't have their names, but we would be happy to communicate privately.
So, then what oversight do you have over the veterinarians that the owners choose to examine their horses, which could benefit them if they got a very good health report on their horse?

So the horses need to be licensed in New York state and to sign off under their license. But again, to just

remind everybody, we are here to support the intent of this bill.
Okay, thank you.
We are here to provide reasons why the intent of this bill is necessary. Thank you.
Thank you, Council Member. Council Member De La Rosa?

Thank you, Chair. First, I want to thank the Chair and the Speaker for their leadership on this issue. Certainly one that is important for us to be taking up today. I'm the former Labor Chair of this council, and so last session we had a spirited discussion around labor protections, and it is a part of the bill that I am interested in us digging into. Would you agree, Commissioners, that the horse-drawn carriage industry is part of the tourism industry in New York City?

I think historically it's been a part of the tourist industry in New York City, yes. Even including in new outreach materials that we've developed at the agency pursuant to council legislation, we've incorporated information on horse-drawn carriages.

Great. And I want to also join the choir of council members. I think all of us are reeling over the death of Romanch, and his family's pain is something that we all feel. A lot of us here on the council are parents. Those of us that aren’t parents can certainly see the pain and the anguish in these families' lives after this incident. I want to ask you, however, about other families that have experienced similar deaths in New York City due to tourism-related activities. In April 10th, 2025, a sightseeing helicopter crashed into the Hudson and six tourists in New York City were killed. In July 2021, a pedicab driver was hit by an SUV. The pedicab driver passed, and the two people who were in the pedicabs were injured. Would the administration also be in favor of banning those industries as they exist today in New York City?

Thank you for the question, Councilmember. You know, I think– to answer your question directly, this is not something we're prepared to talk to you about today or– and not something that we've been presented on to discuss. I don't think we're there yet necessarily with those

industries. Albeit I think we're open to any types of reforms, I could say to the pedicab industry, for example. I think when it comes to horse-drawn carriages, I think your initial question, is it a part of the tourist industry in New York City? Yes. I think what this hearing is about is, should it be? And our position is that it should not be. Ultimately, there's a tragic death, and I'm a father as well, and I can't imagine the pain that the family's feeling right now. And on top of that, there's been deaths of animals, and it's seemingly happening every year. After robust efforts that many administrations have made to try and reform this industry, I think we are past the point of reform of the industry, and we're now at a place of looking to wind down the industry, keeping in mind the livelihoods of workers and how we can phase those out responsibly as well.

I appreciate your response. I would urge us to also look at those other industries because one death is one too many, whether it's a human death, an animal death, a person on a helicopter's death. You know, all of these people come to New York City to take advantage of the

amenities that New York City have to offer. And these activities have been part of the cultural and touristic experiences of people who come all over the world to visit our city. So as we look to reform this industry, we should also be taking a look at those other industries. I know Gale is brave and will get in a pedicab, but if an accident happens two years from now in a pedicab in Central Park, then we will be in this same position. And I maintain that if previous administrations would have done what they needed to do, in 2026 we would not be here having this conversation once again. It's easy to say we could have passed a bill one year ago, we could have passed a bill 10 years ago, and still here we are in 2026. So it is on all of us as we legislate to also look at what future industry issues could arise, so that we're not creating a situation where we're ending one industry in exchange for another industry that is equally unsafe.

Well, DCWP, I should say, has never shied away from a hard conversation about what we have to do in the city to improve outcomes for New Yorkers. And in particularly, I would just stress that the ethos of

our agency is to deliver concrete outcomes that improve the lives of New Yorkers. So if that's a conversation that the council wants to have about those industries that we regulate in particular, I am quite willing to have that conversation.
Great. I appreciate it. Thank you.
Thank you. Council Member Feliz?

Thank you. Thank you, Chair, for this hearing, and thank you, DOH and DCWP, for your testimony and for all the work you've been doing on this issue. I just want to start by briefly speaking in favor of the legislation. We've seen a lot of issues related to these horse carriages, animal welfare issues, including horses literally dying in our streets. Also escalating public safety incidents, including the incident that we saw last month. These are issues that cannot be resolved through legislation or reform or training. We have to do what's right. So just want to thank everyone who has joined today and also everyone who has been in this fight since day one. So a few questions first about— on the workers and also then

on the horses. So you mentioned there's approximately 170 workers in the horse carriage industry?

I would say that there are 208 licensed horse carriage drivers. My understanding from some reporting is that not all of those folks are actively engaged in the work. And then, I don't know if we have a count necessarily yet on the amount of folks involved in the stables.
Is this seasonal work, or is it year-round work? And also, what's the general salary?
What was the last part of the question? I'm sorry.
What's their average salary for these workers?

I'm not sure if I'm aware of the salary. I think that would be helpful to learn through this hearing process. I think we see horse-drawn carriages out there throughout the year. Albeit there are limitations when there are severe weather conditions that my colleague referred to on when they can operate. There are also time restrictions that have been put in place. There are geographic restrictions that have

been put in place in this industry over the very many years.
Right, so would you say this is seasonal employment? Let's say like 8 months out of the 12 months per year?
I'm not sure if I can speak to if it's seasonal or not.

Would you say it could potentially be possible to– for example, if it's 200 workers, we obviously have a lot, as you know, we obviously have a lot of vacancies in almost every single city agency. Do you think it could potentially be possible to bring all of these workers to our city agencies, or do we see any obstacles that are foreseeable?

I'm not– I know that the city hiring process itself– I guess it would depend on what role, and certainly people can apply to positions that are available right now. They can sign up for civil service exams right now. These, these– this option already exists for workers across the city.

A few questions related to the horses. How many incidents related to

medical issues have we had in the last more or less two years that you're aware of?

So the administrative code does not require reporting to us of medical incidents. So that is part of the challenge in responding to some of the data questions. We certainly follow the news and get complaints that we follow up on and get referrals from NYPD. The administrative code does not allow horses to be worked when they are ill or injured. So, that's part of why we don't— why we don't have a count. There have been counts in the press of incidents, and we would have those same counts based on our review of new— you know, the news that we monitor.
Okay. Thank you.
Thank you.

Thank you very much. Give us one second. We're trying to see— we think one of our– one of the members is online. We're just trying to check on that. So give us a second. No. Alright. I want to thank the admin. We're going take a five-minute break, and then we're gonna resume with the rest of the testimony. Thank you.
Thank you, Chair. [break]

Ladies and gentlemen, please find your seats. The hearing's about to re-begin. Ladies and gentlemen, quiet on the Floor. Find your seats, please. The hearing's about to start again. Please find your seats. Thank you. Please find your seats. Please take conversations outside. Quiet on the floor, quiet on the floor, please, please find your seats, please find your seats. We will be starting momentarily.
[gavel] Alright, everyone, we're back in session. I want to call up— want to call up State Senator Eric Bottcher.
It's just me up here.
It's just you because you're— I don't know, your colleagues were supposed to come. I don't know where they are, but go ahead.

Good morning, Chair Schulman, members of the committee. Thank you for the opportunity to testify today. I represent New York State District— New York State Senate District 47,

which includes Hell's Kitchen, where the horse carriage stables are located, and parts of Central Park where these carriages operate every day. And every day, I and my colleagues who also represent this district— Council Member Carl Wilson, Council Member Brewer, we witness 1,500-pound animals pulling carriages nose to tailpipe through Manhattan gridlock, behind buses, trucks, taxis, through construction sites. And I've watched this issue unfold firsthand. Our district has been the site of multiple horse carriage deaths. Including Ryder and Lady. And after years of seeing these tragedies repeat themselves, I've reached one unavoidable conclusion: the status quo is not sustainable. And then, of course, we witnessed what so many of us feared would happen eventually— the loss of human life. Romanch came to New York to experience the world's greatest city. Instead, his family experienced the most unimaginable tragedy. His death made clear what many of us have known for years, what the Central Park Conservancy has been saying, that tourist horse carriages are fundamentally incompatible with modern Midtown Manhattan. I want to make a very important point, that this bill is the

best path forward for the workers. Now is the time to help them transition before the industry's decline leaves them with fewer options. Waiting only makes this transition harder. As we move forward, the carriage drivers must be part of this process. They must be kept informed every step of the way and have a seat at the table and be given access to new employment opportunities with the wages, benefits, healthcare, and job security that they do not currently have. Finally, I want to say that it is so important that we do not demonize each other during this process. That includes the drivers, the stable owners, the union, the animal welfare advocates, and the elected officials. I want to thank my former colleagues in the City Council for supporting this legislation. I know firsthand that this is not an easy issue. When I was a sponsor of this bill, I had full-page ads taken out against me in the New York Post, and they were really nasty. But leadership sometimes comes with a political cost, and I want to thank all of you for your courage. And I know that one day we'll look back at this moment and be proud that New York City chose compassion, safety, and

common sense. I urge you to pass this legislation as soon as possible. Thank you very much.

Thank you, Senator. I was— I apologize, I was supposed to read something before the Senator spoke, so I'll do it now. I want to thank the members of the administration who were here earlier. We are now opening the hearing for public testimony. I want to remind members of the public that this is a government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times. As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times. The witness table is reserved for people who wish to testify. No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table. Furthermore, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recording to the Sergeant-at-Arms for inclusion in the hearing record. If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant-at-Arms and wait to be recognized. When recognized, you will have two minutes to speak on Introduction 943. If you have a written— oh. If you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for

the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant-at-Arms. You may also email written testimony to testimony@council.nyc.gov within 72 hours of the adjournment of this hearing. Audio and video recordings will not be accepted. What? Oh, okay. I said— Yeah, no. I'm going to ask Assemblymember Rosenthal to please come up and testify. Thank you. Go ahead.
Turn this on.

Yeah, it's on now. ASSEMBLYMEMBER ROSENTHAL:Great, great. Speaker Menin, Chair Schulman, Council Member Marte, esteemed members of the Health Committee, good afternoon. I'm Assemblymember Linda B. Rosenthal. I'm Chair of the Assembly Housing Committee, and I proudly represent the Upper West Side and parts of Hell's Kitchen, as well as parts of Central Park, where tragically Romach Mahajan, an 18-year-old tourist from India, died after being thrown from a horse carriage on June 17th, 2026. I'm also an ardent animal rights champion who has passed many laws protecting the rights and lives of New York's most defenseless creatures. Yet despite our collective progress, we still have much to accomplish when it

comes to protecting the city's carriage horses from injury and abuse. And the way to safeguard these majestic creatures is to finally phase out the industry by passing Romanch's Law. In 2011, to combat the rising scourge of deaths and injuries of horses on our streets, I introduced state legislation to ban the use of horse carriages. My intention was to spur the city to take action, but up until today, despite promises and agreements, traffic collisions and dead horses, no bill has passed. But no one gave up. Charlie, Tickler, Billy, Blackjack, Lady, Deniz, Spotty, Juliet, Smoothie, Clancy, Tommy, Ayesha, Misty, and Ryder, those are the names of some of the horses that have died in New York City as a result of their forced employment. There have been more than 100 documented incidences of other horses being badly injured on the job. Some have been hit by cars, motorcycles, and buses. Others have been badly spooked, endangering the lives of riders, carriage drivers, pedestrians, and of course the horses themselves. We can't wait for more horses or people to die on the streets in order to act. Cities across the globe have far fewer tourist distractions, have shown us we don't have to tolerate animal abuse to

churn a profit. I will wind up by saying the New York City Council and the administration can put an end to this cruelty once and for all. It's amazing what a change in administration and leadership can do. I applaud Council Member Marte, all the co-sponsors, and of course the Speaker for putting forth this bill that will not only ban this archaic practice, it will also help to transition current carriage drivers into new jobs. One last thing: today would not be possible without the unyielding support and dedication to this issue by all the advocates and to the many horses who have lost their lives. Thank you for honoring the life of Romanch Mahajan. We will ensure that his death will not be in vain. It's high time we join other countries and cities in refusing to accept abuse as the cost of doing business. Thank you so much.
Thank you very much, Assemblymember. [applause]

No, no clapping, folks, no– you can go like this, but no clapping. Alright. Okay. Okay, now I'm going to call up the next panel, which is Ashley Byrne, Ashley Byrne.

Ashley Byrne here? Edie Falco? Bob Holden? Edita? Birnkrant? Oh, and then this is going to be a hybrid panel, folks. We also have somebody— Dr. Craig Kulikowski [sp?] is going to be joining us remotely. Yeah, sure. Who's going first? Edita? Yeah, go ahead.

Thank you, members. My name is Ashley Byrne, and I am here speaking on behalf of People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals. You cannot regulate the abuse and danger out of the horse-drawn carriage industry. It is cruel and reckless to force a horse, a prey animal, to live and work in the noise, traffic, and chaos of New York City. The carriage operators fight and flout the most mild and common-sense rules with little to no enforcement from the city, as you've heard today. Oversight is almost nonexistent. Lame, sick, emaciated, elderly horses are regularly documented being forced to pull carriages. This hearing is taking place in the middle of what has already proved to be a deadly summer delivered by the horse-drawn carriage industry. The life of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan was tragically added to the long death toll of horses whose lives have been claimed by this industry. Some are names that we know well. The

footage of Ryder, Lady, and Deniz collapsing in our streets sparked widespread outrage and calls for a ban. Many more have died in anonymity, often sold to slaughter after spending their days in traffic being worked to exhaustion and their nights in cramped, solitary parking garage-like buildings, denied everything natural, enriching, and comforting to them. New Yorkers have been fed up with this cruel, deadly industry for years, and polls have consistently shown that New Yorkers want the carriages banned. We applaud Speaker Julie Menin for listening to New Yorkers and taking courageous action to move this ban forward. Thank you to Council Member Christopher Marte for sponsoring the bill, to Committee Chair Lynn Schulman for holding this hearing, and to the committee members for your strong inquiries into the practices of this industry. And to the family of Romanch Mahajan, we send our deepest condolences and gratitude. It's time to pass Romanch's Law.
Thank you. Ms. Falco?
Hi, uh, oops. Like that?
Yes.

Yeah. Hi, my name is Edie Falco. I am an actress and I'm an animal lover and advocate. For some reason I was asked to be here today to tell people how I feel about this. And I think I'm going to go way out on a limb here and say from the deepest part of my heart, these animals are not ours. These animals are not ours. They are not put on this planet to do our bidding. They're not for us to look at and say, “Oh, that one's going to pull me through the park, and this one I'm going to eat. And this one I'm going to wear, and this one I'm gonna experiment on for drugs.” You know, this is the wrong meeting for this perhaps, but insofar as my animal advocacy, these are not our animals. They have the right to a God-given, if that's what you believe, life just as we do. I have a fantasy of us looking back on this in 200 years and saying, “Remember that when we had those big, beautiful, majestic animals pulling us on carriages?” The fact that there's anybody in this room that can look at an animal with the apparatus and the carriage and the people in the traffic and the sounds and the smells and the heat and say, sure, yeah, that's reasonable. The first time I saw that 40 years ago, I thought, what is

this? It's 40 years later. I've looked face to face with politicians in this city since then who have said, “No, we're on it, we're on it. It's our platform. We're going to make it happen.” To be here, I'm going to say very quickly– I'm an empath. It's what I do for a living, and I can't always turn it off. And to listen to the Romanch's family and what they are going through knocked the wind out of me. I have an 18-year-old, and I came to this city as an 18-year-old with dreams and a life to start. It's 40 years later, and I've lived that dream 4,000 times over, and that I am here with the honor of potentially naming this law for Romanch, for the future he will not have and the dreams he will not get to realize, is the greatest honor of my lifetime. It's time, everybody. It's time. It's time. You can't pretend that you don't know what you know. That's it. Sorry. Thank you.
No, thank you very much. Bob Holden? Mr. Holden?

Yes, and good afternoon, Chair, and thank you for this hearing. And I want to thank Speaker Menin and Chris Marte for taking up the banner. My name is Bob Holden, and I had the honor of

representing District 30 in Queens from 2018 to 2025. And I'm the original author of the legislation before you today, the bill that began as Ryder's Law and is now rightfully Romanch's Law. I introduced this bill in 2022 after a horse named Ryder, nearly 30 years old, malnourished and suffering a disease, collapsed on 9th Avenue in a heat wave while his driver struck him with the reins. I spent the next four years begging the Council, the former Council that preceded this, for a hearing. Four years trying to get a hearing. Adrienne Adams, the Speaker, refused to allow it, flat out. And I was told that, that it would never get heard. A deal was made. Year after year, she personally blocked this bill from reaching the floor. No hearing, no vote, no voice. 70 percent of New Yorkers who supported it, they had no voice. The Conservancy, Central Park Conservancy supports it, endorsed it. The Mayor endorsed it. She still said no. Now I'm going to say something that's difficult to say, and the family, I know, is here, and my original bill would have banned horse-drawn carriages in New York City on June 1st of this year. Romanch died on June 17th. That should be chilling to the members listening. 16 days we're talking about.

That is the cost of four years of obstruction. An 18-year-old boy on his family's first trip to America celebrating his graduation is gone because this industry was allowed to keep operating 16 days past the date my bill would have shut it down. The hearing I fought for four years is now happening. The bill is in front of you. The public is behind you. Pass Romanch's law now. Thank you very much.
Thank you. Edita?

Thank you, Committee. My name is Edita Birnkrant, Executive Director of NYCLASS. For more than a decade I've documented and reported the dangers of horse carriages, but today, rather than repeat any of that, I want to amplify a voice that deserves this council's attention. Anita McGill, whose family owned and operated Chateau Stables, once the largest horse stable in New York City for nearly 50 years, reached out to me because she says several carriage owners are now desperate for a way to leave this business before a ban goes into effect. “My name is Anita McGill. I am part of Chateau Stables, my family's business. We owned the largest fleet of horse and carriages at our stable at 608 West 48th Street. In 2018, we sold our stable and

semi-retired to our family farm. I've been asked to submit a statement by some current horse and carriage owners to seek some relief and get help for them to be offered an option to get out of the carriage business. My opinion talking with them is the quaint leisure horse and carriage ride is no longer like it used to be. They are now squeezing past CitiBikes, pedicabs, runners, baby strollers, and millions of extra park-goers. This is a safety issue. I feel there are no more safety solutions that can be applied to lower the risk of more and more accidents happening. Frederick Olmsted designed the park to be seen by horse and carriage. Yes, he did, but not in 2026. Central Park is totally different just in the past 10 years. It's exploded with millions more population and traffic. Business is way down, I hear from some owners. There is nobody applying for a horse and carriage license. Owners struggle to pay the board. What is the benefit? I hope the city allows the horse and carriage owners to get out graciously and compensate them so that they and their horses can live peacefully.” Also, she made a point about hitching posts which Council Member Gennaro is obsessed with. Hitching posts to me are only a recipe

for more problems. It encourages drivers to walk away and leave the horses alone. Not every horse accepts being tethered. They can feel tension, panic, and back up and bust up what's behind them. Horses can rub their bridles off on hitching posts, creating a whole different set of problems. So I think, you know, please pass Romanch's Law, Intro 943. No more tragedies. Thank you.

Alright, before this panel goes anywhere, we have some council members that have questions. Council Member— Oh, I'm sorry, we have— sorry, we have the hybrid. I forgot. Dr. Craig Kulikowski, you have 2 minutes. Is he there? They don't— Dr. Kulikowski, are you online? He is? Do we have— are we having technical issues? Because he says he's online. Alright, we'll come back to him. In the meantime, Council Member Wong has questions, and we have another councilmember also with questions.

Yes. Thank you, Chair. Councilman Holden, I still call you Councilman. Critics of this bill have argued it would destroy jobs, and when I was getting my water, someone also said— told me the same thing. As the

original author of the workforce provisions in this legislation, what is your response to that argument?

Well, first of all, there's a— there's some lies out there. Most of the drivers, the vast majority are independent contractors. That means they're not getting benefits. I'd like to know, I've asked TWU, how many union members actually are drivers, real drivers, independent contractors? How many are paying union dues? And what benefits do they get? So right now, I would say, in just talking to some of the drivers, they don't get any benefits. If they have city jobs, well-paying city jobs, they'll get health coverage, a pension, and they'll get other things that go along with regular jobs. It's a big scam that's going on. And why does— if the TWU would just reveal how many dues-paying union members they have, we might get somewhere. But we won't get that. I never got that in four years, over four years of actually trying to get some movement on this bill. So there's not great-paying jobs out there. These are day workers or independent contractors.
Okay, thank you. Thank you, Chair.
Okay, um, Council Member Gennaro?

Thank you, Madam Chair. I think I'm going to start to– from my right and go left. I wrote down some of the names. First would be to Ashley from PETA. When you found out, or when PETA found out that Deniz had— the horse Deniz had died from eating toxic Japanese yew plants. You being a premier animal rights organization, did you do anything?

Yes, we pointed out that Deniz never should have been in Central Park in the first place, and that if his driver was attending to him properly, he wouldn't have been eating the vegetation in the first place.
Did you—
[interposing] And if his driver was following regulations, he wouldn't have eaten the vegetation.

Well, let's kind of expand this a little bit. So we have toxic plants in the park that are toxic to every species that is native to the park, species that migrate through the park, people walking their dogs in the park, stray

cats, whatever. Every single animal is subject to being poisoned or killed by Japanese yew. And as an animal rights organization, did you say anything to the Central Park Conservancy about this was not the kind of plant that should be in a park with such a diverse array of animals? Did you address the Conservancy? Forget about the horses right now because, you know, Deniz is already dead. Andn so– and I, you know, as someone who's been an equestrian for 60 years, I know that horses graze. Have you ever driven by a field of horses where even one was not grazing? That's not how this works. But anyway, moving to other animals. Did you have any concerns about any of the other animals in the park which your agency is supposedly all about. Yes or no?
Actually, what you just pointed out about horses grazing is precisely one of the reasons—
[interposing] Could you please answer my question?
they don’t belong in Central Park.
Did you—
[interposing] They’re denied everything that–
Did you— PETA— did you—
[interposing] are forced to be in an environment where they—
[interposing] Hey, I get to ask the questions and you answer my questions. So my question is, did PETA do anything about the presence of toxic plants in the park?
Are you asking if we started a campaign to ban a plant? [applause]
No clapping. No clapping, guys.
I asked the questions here, and–
[interposing] Come on.

when I heard about the plants, I issued a statement, I put in a bill request about toxic plants in New York City parks, and I wrote the— and I wrote the, you know,

Central Park Conservancy. So I guess I'm more of an animal lover than you are. Edie Falco.
That's cute, but—
Edie Falco— no, no, no, I'm done with my question with you.
The fact is the horse should not have been in the park–
I’m done.
to eat the plants in the first place.
Edie Falco.
Council Member Gennaro, your time is up. Council Member Hanif?

Thank you. I want to just first say to Edie, I'm a big fan. And I love The Sopranos. It is my favorite show. I would love to hear from you. How do you respond to people who are– who believe that supporting horse welfare and supporting carriage drivers are mutually exclusive? Why do you think it's important to care about both?
